claims.text: The studied material is equiatomic FeNiCrMn.
The initial FeNiCrMn crystal is single-phase FCC.
The initial crystal contains no pre-existing vacancy clusters or HCP regions.
Plastic yielding is initiated by thermally activated kink-pair nucleation on screw dislocations.
Kink-pair formation on screw dislocations is the rate-limiting step for plasticity.
Shockley partial dislocations create intrinsic stacking faults and carry the deformation.
Increasing temperature lowers the free-energy barrier for kink-pair nucleation and reduces the critical stress approximately exponentially.
Higher strain rates produce higher dislocation densities because there is insufficient time for dislocation annihilation.
Yield stress is relatively insensitive to strain rate from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
The strain-rate insensitivity of yield stress occurs because the thermally activated nucleation barrier, rather than dislocation-annihilation kinetics, controls yielding.
Yield strength decreases monotonically as temperature increases from 300 to 1000 K.
Loading along <11-1> gives a larger Schmid factor for the active slip system than loading along <110>.
The <11-1> orientation exhibits a higher peak yield stress than the <110> orientation.
The HCP-like regions produced during deformation are intrinsic stacking faults rather than a transformed HCP phase.
The HCP-like regions will disappear after unloading or annealing.
A true phase transformation would produce persistent long-range HCP order or a distinct lattice-parameter shift.
The stacking-fault energy of FCC FeNiCrMn is low enough to favor partial-dislocation emission but high enough to prevent spontaneous HCP transformation under the simulated conditions.
No deformation twinning or FCC-to-BCC transformation occurs under the stated conditions.
The role of vacancy clusters or other pre-existing defects in dislocation nucleation remains uncertain.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says that <11-1> maximizes the Schmid factor yet also predicts a higher applied peak yield stress for this orientation. For the same CRSS, a larger Schmid factor normally implies a lower required applied stress, so the stated orientation mechanism does not coherently produce the predicted ordering.
